claim: GJA1 mRNA undergoes internal translation to generate N-terminal truncated isoforms of Connexin43 with the predominant isoform being only 20 kDa in size (GJA1-20k).
source: The Connexin43 gap junction gene GJA1 has one coding exon, but its mRNA undergoes internal translation to generate N-terminal truncated isoforms of Connexin43 with the predominant isoform being only 20 kDa in size (GJA1-20k).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and is part of established knowledge about GJA1.

claim: Endogenous GJA1-20k protein is not membrane bound.
source: Endogenous GJA1-20k protein is not membrane bound and has been found to increase in response to ischemic stress, localize to mitochondria, and mimic ischemic preconditioning protection in the heart.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about GJA1-20k properties.

claim: GJA1-20k has been found to increase in response to ischemic stress.
source: Endogenous GJA1-20k protein is not membrane bound and has been found to increase in response to ischemic stress, localize to mitochondria, and mimic ischemic preconditioning protection in the heart.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research findings.

claim: GJA1-20k localizes to mitochondria.
source: Endogenous GJA1-20k protein is not membrane bound and has been found to increase in response to ischemic stress, localize to mitochondria, and mimic ischemic preconditioning protection in the heart.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding about GJA1-20k.

claim: GJA1-20k mimics ischemic preconditioning protection in the heart.
source: Endogenous GJA1-20k protein is not membrane bound and has been found to increase in response to ischemic stress, localize to mitochondria, and mimic ischemic preconditioning protection in the heart.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research findings.

claim: GJA1-20k polymerizes actin around mitochondria which induces focal constriction sites.
source: Here, using human cells and mice, we identify that GJA1-20k polymerizes actin around mitochondria which induces focal constriction sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Mitochondrial fission events occur within about 45 s of GJA1-20k recruitment of actin.
source: Mitochondrial fission events occur within about 45 s of GJA1-20k recruitment of actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4G and Videos 1-3.

claim: GJA1-20k mediated fission is independent of canonical Dynamin-Related Protein 1 (DRP1).
source: Interestingly, GJA1-20k mediated fission is independent of canonical Dynamin-Related Protein 1 (DRP1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing fission occurs even with DRP1 inhibition (Figure 2, Figure 4).

claim: GJA1-20k-induced smaller mitochondria have decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation.
source: We find that GJA1-20k-induced smaller mitochondria have decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and, in hearts, provide potent protection against ischemia-reperfusion injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: GJA1-20k-induced smaller mitochondria provide potent protection against ischemia-reperfusion injury in hearts.
source: We find that GJA1-20k-induced smaller mitochondria have decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and, in hearts, provide potent protection against ischemia-reperfusion injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Stress responsive internally translated GJA1-20k stabilizes polymerized actin filaments to stimulate non-canonical mitochondrial fission which limits ischemic-reperfusion induced myocardial infarction.
source: The results indicate that stress responsive internally translated GJA1-20k stabilizes polymerized actin filaments to stimulate non-canonical mitochondrial fission which limits ischemic-reperfusion induced myocardial infarction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ischemia-Reperfusion (I/R) injury induces excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) in mitochondria, which results in cellular dysfunction and organ damage.
source: Ischemia-Reperfusion (I/R) injury is known to induce excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) in mitochondria, which results in cellular dysfunction and organ damage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ischemic preconditioning was first described 35 years ago.
source: Interestingly, the phenomenon of ischemic preconditioning, first described 35 years ago (Murry et al., 1986), is a potent yet ironic protection of organs from ischemia-induced damage achieved by preceding the full ischemic insult with shorter bouts of ischemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murry et al., 1986.

claim: Ischemic preconditioning is a potent protection of organs from ischemia-induced damage achieved by preceding the full ischemic insult with shorter bouts of ischemia.
source: Interestingly, the phenomenon of ischemic preconditioning, first described 35 years ago (Murry et al., 1986), is a potent yet ironic protection of organs from ischemia-induced damage achieved by preceding the full ischemic insult with shorter bouts of ischemia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The mechanisms of preconditioning are not well understood.
source: Despite the large therapeutic potential of preconditioning for any organ such as heart, kidney, skeletal muscle, or brain subjected to anticipated ischemia, the mechanisms of preconditioning are not well understood, nor has an intervention been identified to successfully translate the phenomenon into clinical utility (Heusch and Gersh, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge supported by citation.

claim: No intervention has been identified to successfully translate the phenomenon of preconditioning into clinical utility.
source: Despite the large therapeutic potential of preconditioning for any organ such as heart, kidney, skeletal muscle, or brain subjected to anticipated ischemia, the mechanisms of preconditioning are not well understood, nor has an intervention been identified to successfully translate the phenomenon into clinical utility (Heusch and Gersh, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mitochondria undergo both fission and fusion in an adaptive equilibrium which directly affects cellular activity and response to stress.
source: Mitochondria undergo both fission and fusion in an adaptive equilibrium which directly affects cellular activity and response to stress (Youle and van der Bliek, 2012; Friedman and Nunnari, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondrial fission can be a causative element of ROS generation, apoptosis, cellular senescence, and cell death.
source: For instance, is mitochondrial fission a causative element of ROS generation, apoptosis, cellular senescence, and cell death (Suen et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2017; Nishimura et al., 2018), or is fission actually protective, such as by promoting mitophagy which can promote survival (Shirakabe et al., 2016; Burman et al., 2017)?
evidence: This is stated as a possibility supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mitochondrial fission can be protective by promoting mitophagy which can promote survival.
source: For instance, is mitochondrial fission a causative element of ROS generation, apoptosis, cellular senescence, and cell death (Suen et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2017; Nishimura et al., 2018), or is fission actually protective, such as by promoting mitophagy which can promote survival (Shirakabe et al., 2016; Burman et al., 2017)?
evidence: This is stated as a possibility supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both the gap junction protein Connexin43 (Cx43) and mitochondria are associated with preconditioning protection.
source: Both the gap junction protein Connexin43 (Cx43) and mitochondria are associated with preconditioning protection (Garcia-Dorado et al., 2006; Basheer et al., 2018; Rodriguez-Sinovas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1 has a single coding exon and thus is not subject to splicing.
source: GJA1, which encodes Cx43, has a single coding exon and thus is not subject to splicing (Smyth and Shaw, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GJA1 mRNA is subject to endogenous internal translation generating several N-terminal truncated isoforms.
source: However, GJA1 mRNA is subject to endogenous internal translation generating several N-terminal truncated isoforms (Smyth and Shaw, 2013; Salat-Canela, 2014; Ul-Hussain et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k contains the full Cx43 C-terminus but lacks transmembrane domains.
source: GJA1-20k, which contains the full Cx43 C-terminus but lacks transmembrane domains, is the most abundant and most common smaller isoform and is essential to full-length Cx43 trafficking (Smyth and Shaw, 2013; Xiao et al., 2020) by recruiting cytoplasmic actin to organize trafficking pathways (Basheer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k is the most abundant and most common smaller isoform of GJA1.
source: GJA1-20k, which contains the full Cx43 C-terminus but lacks transmembrane domains, is the most abundant and most common smaller isoform and is essential to full-length Cx43 trafficking (Smyth and Shaw, 2013; Xiao et al., 2020) by recruiting cytoplasmic actin to organize trafficking pathways (Basheer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k is essential to full-length Cx43 trafficking.
source: GJA1-20k, which contains the full Cx43 C-terminus but lacks transmembrane domains, is the most abundant and most common smaller isoform and is essential to full-length Cx43 trafficking (Smyth and Shaw, 2013; Xiao et al., 2020) by recruiting cytoplasmic actin to organize trafficking pathways (Basheer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k recruits cytoplasmic actin to organize trafficking pathways.
source: GJA1-20k, which contains the full Cx43 C-terminus but lacks transmembrane domains, is the most abundant and most common smaller isoform and is essential to full-length Cx43 trafficking (Smyth and Shaw, 2013; Xiao et al., 2020) by recruiting cytoplasmic actin to organize trafficking pathways (Basheer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GJA1-20k is highly enriched at the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: In addition, GJA1-20k is highly enriched at the outer mitochondrial membrane (Fu et al., 2017; Basheer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k abundance increases with hypoxic and ischemic stress.
source: GJA1-20k abundance increases with hypoxic and ischemic stress (Basheer et al., 2018), resulting in a phenotypically profound cardiac protection that mimics ischemic preconditioning (Basheer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Increased GJA1-20k results in a phenotypically profound cardiac protection that mimics ischemic preconditioning.
source: GJA1-20k abundance increases with hypoxic and ischemic stress (Basheer et al., 2018), resulting in a phenotypically profound cardiac protection that mimics ischemic preconditioning (Basheer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k expression in HEK293 cells results in a 54% decrease in average mitochondrial area.
source: GJA1-20k co-localizes with mitochondria and its presence results in a more rounded and punctate appearance of the mitochondria. GJA1-20k also induces a 54% decrease in average mitochondrial area (Figure 1A and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and F.

claim: siRNA-mediated knock-down of GJA1 expression increases mitochondrial area by 20%.
source: siRNA-mediated knock-down of GJA1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) conversely increases mitochondrial area by 20% (Figure 1B and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and F.

claim: Mitochondrial size after GJA1 knock-down can be rescued by siRNA-resistant GJA1-20k overexpression.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial size after GJA1 knock-down can be rescued by siRNA-resistant GJA1-20k overexpression, but not with overexpression of siRNA resistant Cx43-M6L, which expresses full-length Cx43 without the truncated isoforms (Smyth and Shaw, 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Mitochondrial size after GJA1 knock-down cannot be rescued by overexpression of siRNA resistant Cx43-M6L, which expresses full-length Cx43 without the truncated isoforms.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial size after GJA1 knock-down can be rescued by siRNA-resistant GJA1-20k overexpression, but not with overexpression of siRNA resistant Cx43-M6L, which expresses full-length Cx43 without the truncated isoforms (Smyth and Shaw, 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The short GJA1-20k isoform, but not full-length Cx43, reduces mitochondrial size.
source: Together, these data suggest that the short GJA1-20k isoform, but not full-length Cx43, reduces mitochondrial size.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated GJA1-20k overexpression in wild type neonatal mouse cardiomyocytes results in a decrease in the average mitochondria area.
source: We overexpressed GJA1-20k by adenovirus transduction in wild type (WT) neonatal mouse CMs and found a decrease in the average mitochondria area (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: Neonatal cardiomyocytes from Gja1M213L/M213L mice have an increase in their average area of mitochondria.
source: Neonatal CMs from Gja1M213L/M213L mice have an increase in their average area of mitochondria (Figure 1C and F), in contrast to the decrease in mitochondrial area of neonatal CMs with GJA1-20k overexpression (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: The Gja1M213L/M213L mutation removes the internal translation start site, resulting in expression of full length Cx43 protein but not the internally translated GJA1-20k isoform.
source: We then used neonatal CMs from a Gja1M213L/M213L mouse line that was recently generated by mutating the internal AUG (Methionine) at residue 213 of Gja1 to UUA (Leucine). This M213L mutation removes the internal translation start site, resulting in expression of full length Cx43 protein but not the internally translated GJA1-20k isoform (Xiao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the mouse model supported by citation.

claim: The mitochondria of 2-week-old cardiomyocytes deficient of GJA1-20k are enlarged.
source: The mitochondria of 2-week-old cardiomyocytes deficient of GJA1-20k are enlarged (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: Homozygous Gja1M213L/M213L mice die from poor gap junction trafficking and arrhythmogenic sudden cardiac death two to four weeks after birth.
source: The homozygous Gja1M213L/M213L mice, which lack the expression of GJA1-20k but not full-length Cx43, die from poor gap junction trafficking and arrhythmogenic sudden cardiac death two to four weeks after birth (Xiao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the mouse model supported by citation.

claim: AAV9-mediated delivery of exogenous GJA1-20k to 8 week old adult WT mice results in a decrease in the average mitochondrial area.
source: We then delivered exogenous GJA1-20k using adeno-associated virus type 9 (AAV9) to 8 week old adult WT mice (Basheer et al., 2018) and found a decrease in the average mitochondrial area (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: In cell lines, neonatal CM, young mouse hearts, and mature mouse hearts, an increase in GJA1-20k results in smaller mitochondria, whereas a decrease in GJA1-20k results in larger mitochondria.
source: Taken together, in cell lines, neonatal CM, young mouse hearts, and mature mouse hearts, an increase in GJA1-20k results in smaller mitochondria, whereas a decrease in GJA1-20k results in larger mitochondria.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings shown in Figure 1.

claim: GJA1-20k is involved in mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Previously, we reported that GJA1-20k is involved in mitochondrial biogenesis (Basheer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding supported by citation.

claim: AAV9-transduced adult cardiomyocytes showed increased mitochondrial DNA copy number.
source: Consistent with our previous study, AAV9-transduced adult cardiomyocytes showed increased mitochondrial DNA copy number and GJA1-20k deficient mice (Gja1M213L/M213L) had decreased copy number.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: GJA1-20k deficient mice (Gja1M213L/M213L) had decreased mitochondrial DNA copy number.
source: Consistent with our previous study, AAV9-transduced adult cardiomyocytes showed increased mitochondrial DNA copy number and GJA1-20k deficient mice (Gja1M213L/M213L) had decreased copy number.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Exogenous GJA1-20k did not alter the mitochondrial biogenesis in HEK293 cells.
source: However, exogenous GJA1-20k did not alter the mitochondrial biogenesis in HEK293 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Exogenous GJA1-20k did not affect membrane potential in HEK293 cells.
source: Nor did exogenous GJA1-20k affect membrane potential or baseline ATP production (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Exogenous GJA1-20k did not affect baseline ATP production in HEK293 cells.
source: Nor did exogenous GJA1-20k affect membrane potential or baseline ATP production (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Neither biogenesis nor mitophagy protein markers were altered in GJA1-20k transfected HEK293 cells.
source: In addition to mitochondrial DNA copy number, neither biogenesis nor mitophagy protein markers were altered in either GJA1-20k transfected HEK293 cells or Gja1M213L/M213L mouse hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Neither biogenesis nor mitophagy protein markers were altered in Gja1M213L/M213L mouse hearts.
source: In addition to mitochondrial DNA copy number, neither biogenesis nor mitophagy protein markers were altered in either GJA1-20k transfected HEK293 cells or Gja1M213L/M213L mouse hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F-G.

claim: Mitochondrial dynamics are regulated by DRP1 for fission.
source: Mitochondrial dynamics are regulated by well-known mediators including DRP1 for fission (Friedman and Nunnari, 2014), and MFN1 and MFN2 for fusion (Schrepfer and Scorrano, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondrial dynamics are regulated by MFN1 and MFN2 for fusion.
source: Mitochondrial dynamics are regulated by well-known mediators including DRP1 for fission (Friedman and Nunnari, 2014), and MFN1 and MFN2 for fusion (Schrepfer and Scorrano, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DRP1 is potentiated by phosphorylation of its Serine 616 and 637.
source: DRP1 is potentiated by phosphorylation of its Serine 616 and 637 (Sabouny and Shutt, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GJA1-20k transfection in HEK293 cells does not significantly change the protein levels of total DRP1, DRP1-pS616, -pS637, or the ratio (pS616/total).
source: We tested abundance of total DRP1 and phosphorylated DRP1 in GJA1-20k transfected HEK293 cells and found no significant difference in either the protein levels of total DRP1, DRP1-pS616, -pS637, or in the ratio (pS616/total) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The levels of MFN1 and MFN2 were unchanged in GJA1-20k transfected HEK293 cells.
source: The levels of MFN1 and MFN2, and mitochondrial marker protein TOM20, a marker of cellular mitochondrial content, were also unchanged (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The levels of mitochondrial marker protein TOM20 were unchanged in GJA1-20k transfected HEK293 cells.
source: The levels of MFN1 and MFN2, and mitochondrial marker protein TOM20, a marker of cellular mitochondrial content, were also unchanged (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: DRP1 inhibition by siRNA-mediated DRP1 knock-down increases the average area of individual mitochondria.
source: With either method of DRP1 inhibition, the average area of individual mitochondria increased, consistent with inhibiting canonical fission (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: DRP1 inhibition by transfecting DRP1 dominant negative mutant (K38A) increases the average area of individual mitochondria.
source: With either method of DRP1 inhibition, the average area of individual mitochondria increased, consistent with inhibiting canonical fission (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: K38A has more pronounced DRP1 inhibition which resulted in greater mitochondrial enlargement than siDRP1.
source: In addition, K38A has more pronounced DRP1 inhibition which resulted in greater mitochondrial enlargement than siDRP1 (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: GJA1-20k acts epistatically to DRP1 loss or interference and prevents DRP1-mediated mitochondrial enlargement.
source: However, GJA1-20k acts epistatically to DRP1 loss or interference and prevents DRP1-mediated mitochondrial enlargement (Figure 2C–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating GJA1-20k can act at or downstream of DRP1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: GJA1-20k can act at or downstream of DRP1 activation.
source: However, GJA1-20k acts epistatically to DRP1 loss or interference and prevents DRP1-mediated mitochondrial enlargement (Figure 2C–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating GJA1-20k can act at or downstream of DRP1 activation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing GJA1-20k prevents DRP1-mediated effects.

claim: Treatment with mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) results in the same effects of GJA1-20k to rescue the dynamics.
source: We also interfered mitochondrial dynamics by treating cells pharmacologically with mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) and found same effects of GJA1-20k to rescue the dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: siDNM2 alone did not affect mitochondrial morphology.
source: In contrast to siDRP1, siDNM2 alone did not affect mitochondrial morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I), with or without GJA1-20k, suggesting no involvement of DNM2 in mitochondrial dynamics of HEK293 cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I.

claim: DNM2 is not necessary to be responsible for mitochondrial fission in some cell lines.
source: It has been reported that DNM2 is not necessary to be responsible for mitochondrial fission in other cell lines as well (Fonseca et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DNM2 is not an essential co-factor in GJA1-20k-mediated mitochondrial fission.
source: The fact that DNM2 is not needed for GJA1-20k activity to occur, indicates it is not an essential co-factor in GJA1-20k-mediated mitochondrial fission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing DNM2 knockdown does not affect GJA1-20k activity.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton and its dynamics have been implicated as fundamental mediators of mitochondrial fission.
source: The actin cytoskeleton and its dynamics have been implicated as fundamental mediators of mitochondrial fission (Korobova et al., 2013; Hatch et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k has been previously identified to cluster with and stabilize the actin network both in vitro and in vivo.
source: GJA1-20k has been previously identified to cluster with and stabilize the actin network both in vitro and in vivo (Basheer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the presence of GJA1-20k, actin assembles around mitochondria, forming filamentous rings surrounding the outer membrane.
source: We imaged actin in GJA1-20k transfected HEK293 cells and noted that, in the presence of GJA1-20k, actin assembles around mitochondria, forming filamentous rings surrounding the outer membrane (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GJA1-20k induces a large increase in mitochondrial associated actin.
source: Cytosolic and mitochondrial pools of proteins were separated and actin protein levels were measured in each fraction. As seen in Figure 3B and C, the large increase in mitochondrial associated actin occurs in the presence of GJA1-20k.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: GJA1-20k recruits the actin cytoskeleton to the mitochondrial membrane.
source: Together these data provide both imaging and biochemical evidence that GJA1-20k recruits the actin cytoskeleton to the mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and biochemical data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: GJA1-20k does not directly promote actin polymerization.
source: Using a reductionist cell-free assay of actin polymerization, we found that GJA1-20k does not directly promote actin polymerization (Figure 3D), and the polymerization kinetics is even slightly slowed down in the presence of GJA1-20K.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The polymerization kinetics is slightly slowed down in the presence of GJA1-20K.
source: Using a reductionist cell-free assay of actin polymerization, we found that GJA1-20k does not directly promote actin polymerization (Figure 3D), and the polymerization kinetics is even slightly slowed down in the presence of GJA1-20K.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GJA1-20k directly inhibits actin depolymerization.
source: However, GJA1-20k causes a leftward shift in the polymerization-depolymerization equilibrium (Blanchoin et al., 2014) by directly inhibiting actin depolymerization (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GJA1-20k causes a leftward shift in the polymerization-depolymerization equilibrium.
source: However, GJA1-20k causes a leftward shift in the polymerization-depolymerization equilibrium (Blanchoin et al., 2014) by directly inhibiting actin depolymerization (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 3E and citation.

claim: The effect of substantial GJA1-20k, by inhibiting depolymerization, is to cause a net increase in polymerization.
source: The effect of substantial GJA1-20k, by inhibiting depolymerization, is to cause a net increase in polymerization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the depolymerization inhibition data.

claim: GJA1-20k enriches at outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: Because GJA1-20k enriches at outer mitochondrial membrane (Fu et al., 2017; Basheer et al., 2018), the GJA1-20k-induced polymerization will occur at and around the mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GJA1-20k-induced polymerization will occur at and around the mitochondrial membrane.
source: Because GJA1-20k enriches at outer mitochondrial membrane (Fu et al., 2017; Basheer et al., 2018), the GJA1-20k-induced polymerization will occur at and around the mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on GJA1-20k localization and its effect on actin.

claim: GJA1-20k results in net actin polymerization even in the presence of Latrunculin A (LatA).
source: Interestingly, GJA1-20k results in net actin polymerization even in the presence of Latrunculin A (LatA), a known potent inhibitor of actin polymerization (Fujiwara et al., 2018; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Latrunculin A (LatA) is a known potent inhibitor of actin polymerization.
source: Interestingly, GJA1-20k results in net actin polymerization even in the presence of Latrunculin A (LatA), a known potent inhibitor of actin polymerization (Fujiwara et al., 2018; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LatA increases individual mitochondrial area, consistent with an inhibition of actin-dependent mitochondrial fission.
source: In cells, it has been reported that LatA increases individual mitochondrial area, consistent with an inhibition of actin-dependent mitochondrial fission (Figure 3F and G; Korobova et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G and citations.

claim: The presence of GJA1-20k counteracts the LatA effect, preserving acting polymerization and preventing an overall increase in mitochondrial size.
source: However, the presence of GJA1-20k counteracts the LatA effect, preserving acting polymerization and preventing an overall increase in mitochondrial size (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Even under siDRP1, actin was assembled around mitochondria by GJA1-20k.
source: To investigate DRP1 involvement in the actin assemble by GJA1-20k, we observed the actin dynamics under siDRP1 treatment. Even under siDRP1, actin was assembled around mitochondria similarly to Figure 3A (Figure 4A), suggesting that DRP1 is not necessary to create actin ring around mitochondria by GJA1-20k.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DRP1 is not necessary to create actin ring around mitochondria by GJA1-20k.
source: To investigate DRP1 involvement in the actin assemble by GJA1-20k, we observed the actin dynamics under siDRP1 treatment. Even under siDRP1, actin was assembled around mitochondria similarly to Figure 3A (Figure 4A), suggesting that DRP1 is not necessary to create actin ring around mitochondria by GJA1-20k.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that actin assembly occurs even with DRP1 knockdown.

claim: GJA1-20k recruits actin to mitochondria, which results in fission.
source: As seen in Video 1 and Figure 4B, GJA1-20k recruits actin to mitochondria, which results in fission.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: Mitochondrial fission occurs at points where the product of GJA1-20k and actin is the highest.
source: The respective line-scan profiles in Figure 4C indicate that mitochondrial fission occurs at points where the product of GJA1-20k and actin is the highest.
evidence: This claim is supported by line-scan analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fission occurs approximately 45 seconds after co-accumulation of GJA1-20k and actin.
source: Fission (low point of blue lines) occurs approximately 45 seconds after co-accumulation of GJA1-20k and actin (high point of red lines, Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Time to fission occurred at a median of 45 seconds, with a standard deviation of 11 seconds.
source: Statistically, this time to fission occurred at a median of 45 seconds, with a standard deviation of 11 seconds (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The mitochondrial fission induced by cooperation between GJA1-20k and actin can be independent of canonical DRP1-mediated fission.
